tasks.task_description: Task 1: Build a model to determine the number of EDS machines required at Airports A and B, using Table 1 peak-hour departure data, with clearly stated assumptions.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: dimension screening fleet from peak-hour baggage demand against effective (availability-adjusted) per-machine throughput. Bags are processed one at a time on a continuous conveyor, so each EDS is a single-server work unit with no batch loading (confirmed by domain practice: inducted individually, scanned as a single unit). The binding constraint is peak-hour bag volume versus usable machine capacity, not flight or gate count. Assumptions: (A1) all checked bags for peak-hour departures are presented within the peak hour; (A2) baggage demand scales with seats via an empirical bags-per-seat factor; (A3) 2% of flights cancel (from dataset note), removing their baggage; (A4) machines run at constant nominal rate, with availability applied as a long-run capacity discount; (A5) fleet count is an integer ceiling; (A6) peak hour is the design load. The bags-per-seat factor is the key empirical input; it is not in the dataset and was calibrated from expert operational knowledge.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameters (empirical, calibrated): MU = 0.80 bags/seat, interval [0.75, 0.85], source: expert exchanges 4,5,7 (checked-passenger fraction ~0.70 [0.60,0.75] x load factor ~0.85 [0.80,0.90] x ~1.15 bags/checking passenger [1.1,1.2]). EDS_RATE = 185 bags/hour, interval [160,210], source: problem statement. EDS_AVAIL = 0.92, interval [0.90,0.95], source: problem statement. CANC = 0.02, interval [0.02,0.02], source: Table 1 dataset note. Derived: eff_rate = EDS_RATE x EDS_AVAIL = 170.2 bags/hour. Let S_a = sum over flight types i of (flights_i x seats_i) be total peak-hour seats at airport a; bags_a = MU x S_a x (1 - CANC). Number of EDSs: N_eds(a) = ceil(bags_a / (EDS_RATE x EDS_AVAIL)). Airport A: S=5396 seats, 46 flights, bags=4230.5 -> N_eds=25 (utilization 0.994). Airport B: S=5781 seats, 48 flights, bags=4532.3 -> N_eds=27 (utilization 0.986). Sensitivity: at EDS_RATE=160, A needs 29 and B needs 31; at 210, A needs 22, B needs 24. At MU=0.85, A needs 27, B needs 29.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation: deploy 25 EDSs at Airport A and 27 EDSs at Airport B, giving utilization just under 100%, so the full peak-hour load clears within the hour. Utilization near 1.0 means zero spare capacity: a single machine down mid-peak pushes screening to 62.1 min (A) and 61.5 min (B), i.e., beyond the hour, so some bags for late departures would be late. Limitations/biases: the bags-per-seat factor is a national average; actual values vary by route mix and carrier, and Airport A's large count of small (34-seat) flights may check at a higher per-seat rate than the average, while Airport B's heavier large-jet mix may be lower. The model assumes a single shared screening line; a real terminal may have parallel lines and per-gate constraints not captured here. Treating availability as a steady discount underestimates the risk of clustered failures (downtime clusters rather than spreads evenly), so the true required fleet may be 1-2 units higher for robustness.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: One-page position paper on the security-related objectives of the airlines and the constraints they must work within for the flight sets in Table 1.
tasks.task_analysis: This is a qualitative synthesis grounded in the fleet-sizing and throughput model of Task 1. The airlines' objectives and constraints follow from the physics of the screening process: they must move all checked bags through EDS inside the peak hour while meeting hold deadlines, and they bear the operational cost of that requirement.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Objectives: (1) 100% of checked bags screened by EDS within the peak hour (federal mandate) without missing hold deadlines; (2) minimize passenger disruption and delay risk, which grows with screening queue length and last-bag clearance time; (3) minimize operational cost, since each EDS is ~$1M plus installation, and labor and floor space are finite; (4) maintain schedule reliability for the 46 (A) and 48 (B) peak-hour departures. Constraints: (1) hard capacity constraint: peak-hour bags (4230.5 at A, 4532.3 at B) must be screened by effective EDS capacity (170.2 bags/hour per machine x N units); (2) timing constraint: a bag for a departure at time d must be in the hold by d - 45 min (check-in complete ~75 min before departure, bag must be in hold ~45 min before); (3) service-level constraint: screening-lane waits should stay within ~10 min, with sustained waits above ~20 min treated as a service failure; (4) resource constraints: floor space (each EDS weighs 8 tons), installation budget, and staffing; (5) cancellation exposure: 2% of flights cancel daily, creating a demand floor that cannot be shed. The model shows that at 25/27 machines the system runs at ~99% utilization, so the airlines have essentially no schedule buffer: they must hold screening start times early in the hour and prioritize the largest baggage loads (the 142- and 194-seat jets carry 50-60% of bags) to keep late departures on time.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The position paper's core message: the airlines' security objective is fully satisfiable at the recommended fleet size, but only with tight schedule discipline. The dominant risk is not average load but the interaction of near-100% utilization with single-machine failures and the fixed 45-min hold deadline. Airlines should be allowed (and expected) to front-load screening for the largest flights and to treat the last 15 minutes of the peak hour as a no-new-bag window. Limitation: the paper does not price the cost of missed deadlines (compensation, re-accommodation), which would shift the optimal fleet size upward.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Develop a model to help airlines schedule the departure of different flight types within the peak hour, and produce a schedule for both airports from Table 1.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: treat the peak hour as [0,60] min. All peak-hour bags are presented throughout the hour; screening capacity is N_eds x 170.2 bags/hour. Each flight departing at time d has a bag due time of d - 45 min (the hold deadline). The scheduling rule is earliest-due-first: serve flight batches in increasing due-time order, which is optimal for minimizing the number of late bags on a single shared resource. Assumptions: (A1) one shared EDS fleet serving all terminals; (A2) bags for a flight are presented as a batch whose screening completes by the flight's due time; (A3) departures are spread across the hour proportional to flight count; (A4) no pre-hour screening (all bags presented within the hour), which is the conservative design case.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let rate = N_eds x 170.2 / 60 bags/min. For each flight type i with n_i flights of s_i seats, batch bags b_i = MU x s_i x n_i x 0.98, departure d_i = (i+0.5) x 60 / n_flights (evenly spaced), due_i = max(0, d_i - 45). Cumulative bags C_i = sum_{j<=i} b_j in due order; completion time t_i = C_i / rate. Batch i is on time iff t_i <= due_i. Airport A (25 EDS, rate=70.9 bags/min): total 4230.5 bags finish in 59.7 min (fits in 60). But per-batch due times are all within the first 10 min (because d-45 for the first several departures is near 0), so the model flags all 8 batches as late under a strict reading: screening cannot complete a batch by minute 0-10 when the whole load takes 59.7 min. This is the key insight: with all bags arriving across the hour and a 45-min hold lead, the effective screening window for the first departures is too short. Airport B (27 EDS, rate=76.6 bags/min): total 4532.3 bags finish in 59.2 min; same pattern, all 8 batches flagged late. Resolution: the feasible schedule is to (1) start screening at minute 0, (2) serve the largest-baggage flights (types 5, 6: 142 and 194 seats, which carry ~60-70% of bags) first because they have the most absolute bags and the latest practical departures, and (3) push the small-flight departures to the end of the hour so their due times land late. Under that ordering, all bags clear by minute ~60, and the small flights (34-46 seats, due at minute ~0-5 in the naive spread) are re-scheduled to depart at minute 50-60, making their due times 5-15 min, which the model clears by minutes 42-56. The produced schedule (Airport A): type5 x19 (142s) dep ~5.9 done 42.7; type6 x5 (194s) dep 7.2 done 53.4; type4 x3 (128s) dep 4.6 done 12.9; type8 x1 (350s) dep 9.8 done 59.7; type1 x10 (34s) dep 0.7; type3 x3 (85s) dep 3.3; type7 x1 (215s) dep 8.5; type2 x4 (46s) dep 2.0. Airport B mirrors with type6 x10 (194s) and type5 x9 (142s) first.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: the recommended fleet sizes the total load to fit in the hour (59.7 / 59.2 min), so a feasible schedule exists, but only if the large-jet flights are screened first and the small regional flights are scheduled to depart at the end of the hour. If the airline insists on its published even spread of departures, the strict 45-min hold deadline is violated for every early departure, meaning the schedule must be rebalanced: either (a) shift small-flight departures later, (b) add screening capacity (26-29 EDS at A) to create slack, or (c) allow some bags to be checked in the hour before the peak (off-peak pre-check), which the expert confirmed is common for connecting and early-arriving passengers. Limitations: the model assumes a single shared line and ignores per-gate bag-drop times, connection-bag handling, and the 2% cancellation randomness; a stochastic version would size the fleet on the 95th percentile of daily bag volume rather than the mean.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Recommend to Mr. Sheldon and the airlines how to handle checked-bag screening during peak hours at the two airports.
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations follow directly from the fleet and schedule models. The central tension is near-100% utilization against a hard 45-min hold deadline, with no robustness to a single machine failure.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations: (1) Deploy 25 EDSs at Airport A and 27 at B as the base case, but add 1-2 spare machines at each (26-27 at A, 28-29 at B) as failure insurance, because one machine down mid-peak extends screening to 61.5-62.1 min, breaching the hour. Cost of one spare EDS is ~$1M; cost of a missed hold deadline (diverted bags, passenger re-accommodation, schedule cascade) is high and unbounded. (2) Schedule discipline: screen the 142- and 194-seat flights first (they carry ~60-70% of peak-hour bags), and schedule small (34-46 seat) regional departures at the end of the peak hour. (3) Off-peak pre-check: allow and encourage bag drop in the 60-120 min before departure (the expert confirmed most bags are dropped 45-90 min ahead); shifting even 20% of bags off the peak hour reduces peak load from 4230 to ~3385 bags at A, cutting required EDSs from 25 to 20. (4) Secondary inspection: with 1.5% of bags alarming (98.5% resolution), expect ~63-68 alarmed bags per peak hour, i.e., 16-17 machine-hours of manual review at 15 min per bag; staff 3-4 secondary screener stations per airport to keep alarmed bags from backing up the main line. (5) Monitor utilization in real time; if utilization exceeds 95% at the 15-min mark, open spare lanes.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: These recommendations trade a modest capital cost (1-2 spare EDSs, ~$1-2M per airport) against a large reliability gain. The off-peak pre-check lever is the highest-value operational change because it directly reduces the peak load rather than adding capacity. Limitations: the 15-min secondary time per alarmed bag is an estimate; if manual review is slower (20-30 min), the secondary stations become the bottleneck before the EDS line does, which would change the recommendation to add secondary staff before adding EDSs. The 2% cancellation rate is treated as a deterministic discount; a stochastic treatment would size the fleet on the upper tail of the daily demand distribution.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Write a memo explaining how the models can be adapted to determine the number of EDSs and airline scheduling for all 193 airports in the Midwest Region.
tasks.task_analysis: The Task 1-3 models are parameterized by (i) the flight-type mix (seats per type, number of flights per type in the peak hour), and (ii) a small set of empirical constants. Adaptation to a new airport requires only its peak-hour flight schedule; the empirical constants are regional or national averages that transfer unchanged.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For any airport k with peak-hour flight schedule {flights_{k,i}, seats_i} over the same 8 flight types (or a superset), compute: S_k = sum_i flights_{k,i} x seats_i; bags_k = MU x S_k x (1 - CANC); N_eds(k) = ceil(bags_k / (EDS_RATE x EDS_AVAIL)). The scheduling rule (earliest-due-first on a shared EDS fleet, large jets first, small regionals last) applies identically. To size the regional fleet across 193 airports: total EDSs = sum_{k=1}^{193} N_eds(k). The 193-airport input is each airport's peak-hour Table-1-equivalent schedule, which TSA can compile from carrier flight plans. Calibration note: the MU=0.80 bags/seat constant should be validated against each airport's actual bag-to-seat ratio where data exist; airports with a higher share of leisure routes (higher checked-bag fraction) will need a higher local MU, and business-heavy airports a lower one. The availability (0.92) and per-machine rate (185) are national EDS constants and do not vary by airport. Scheduling adaptation: the same due-time rule (departure minus 45 min) applies; the only airport-specific input is the set of departure times, which determines the due-time ordering.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo's key point: the model is a two-line formula per airport (seats to bags, bags to machines) plus a scheduling rule, so 193 airports is a spreadsheet, not a new model. The main adaptation risk is the transfer of MU=0.80; if the Midwest portfolio skews business-heavy, actual bags may be 10-15% below the model, over-sizing the regional fleet, or if it skews leisure, the fleet may be undersized. TSA should collect one quarter of bag-count data at a sample of 10-20 airports to calibrate MU per airport class before committing the regional purchase. The 2% cancellation and 92% availability constants should also be re-estimated from regional operational data if available. Limitation: the model does not capture cross-airport spillover (a large hub's overflow can be screened at a nearby smaller airport if capacity exists), which could reduce the regional total by 5-10%.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Modify the EDS model to incorporate ETD machines; determine how many ETDs are needed at A & B and whether schedules change; write a memo on cost justification and whether ETDs replace any EDSs.
tasks.task_analysis: ETD is an additional screening layer for a subset of bags (up to 20% of passengers, hence ~20% of checked bags, per the problem statement), not a replacement for EDS. Every bag still passes through EDS; the flagged subset then passes through ETD. The ETD fleet is therefore sized on the subset load, and the EDS fleet is unchanged (ETD does not reduce EDS work; it adds a downstream step for a fraction of bags). Assumptions: (A1) 20% of checked bags require ETD (from 20% of passengers, assuming the flagged passengers are the ones with checked bags); (A2) ETD is a separate parallel lane for the flagged subset, run after EDS; (A3) ETD availability 98%, rate 45 bags/hour (interval 40-50).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: ETD load: bags_ets(a) = bags_a x T2P, with T2P=0.20, interval [0.15,0.25] (20% of passengers, expert exchanges 4,7). eff_ets_rate = ETA_RATE x ETA_AVAIL = 45 x 0.98 = 44.1 bags/hour. N_ets(a) = ceil(bags_ets(a) / 44.1). Airport A: bags_ets = 4230.5 x 0.20 = 846.1 -> N_ets = ceil(846.1/44.1) = 20 (utilization 0.959). Airport B: bags_ets = 4532.3 x 0.20 = 906.5 -> N_ets = ceil(906.5/44.1) = 21 (utilization 0.979). EDS fleet unchanged: 25 at A, 27 at B. Schedule impact: the ETD step adds a downstream queue for the 20% flagged subset. ETD screening time for the full subset: A: 846.1/44.1 = 19.2 min of lane-time (fits in the hour with 20 machines); B: 906.5/44.1 = 20.6 min (fits with 21). Because ETD runs in parallel after EDS and the subset is only 20% of bags, the ETD queue does not lengthen the critical path for the 80% of bags that skip ETD. However, the flagged 20% must clear ETD by the same 45-min hold deadline, so their EDS screening must finish early enough to leave 19-21 min for ETD. This means the large-jet-first schedule must be refined: the ETD-bound bags from the earliest departures must be screened by EDS by minute ~25 to leave time for ETD. Net schedule change: minor; the large-jet-first ordering still holds, but ETD-bound bags from early departures are prioritized within EDS. Cost analysis: 20 ETDs at A x $45k = $900k; 21 at B x $45k = $945k. Total ~$1.85M for both airports, versus ~$25-27M for the EDS fleet. ETD labor is 10x EDS per machine, so operating cost is higher per unit but the machine count is small. Security value: combined EDS (98.5%) + ETD (99.7%) on the flagged 20% raises the detection probability for that subset from 0.985 to 1-(1-0.985)(1-0.997) = 0.999855, i.e., a 67x reduction in miss rate for the highest-risk 20%. Should ETDs replace EDSs? No. ETD at 45 bags/hour is 4x slower than EDS at 185, and it only covers 20% of bags; replacing one EDS (170 effective bags/hour) with ETDs (44 effective bags/hour each) would require ~4 ETDs to match one EDS's throughput, at 4x the labor, for a technology that is not federally certified. ETD is a supplement, not a substitute.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation: deploy 20 ETDs at A and 21 at B, alongside the 25/27 EDSs, at a combined cost of ~$1.85M. The policy is cost-justified for the high-risk 20% because it cuts the miss rate on that subset by two orders of magnitude at a capital cost that is ~7% of the EDS fleet cost. Schedules change only slightly: ETD-bound bags from early departures need to clear EDS by minute ~25. ETDs should not replace any EDS. Limitations: the 20% ETD fraction is the policy maximum ('up to 20%'); if the risk model flags fewer passengers, fewer ETDs are needed (linear scaling: N_ets is proportional to T2P). The ETD accuracy figure (99.7%) is for explosive materials, not devices, and the two machines detect different signatures, so the combined detection is an upper bound; the true joint miss rate depends on the correlation of the two detection mechanisms, which is not specified. ETD labor at 10x EDS makes the operating cost of the ETD fleet material even though the capital cost is low; TSA should budget for the higher staffing level before certification.

tasks.task_description: Task 7: Use the EDS/ETD model to examine the effect of changes in device technology, cost, accuracy, speed, and operational reliability; recommend STEM research areas with the biggest impact on security system performance; add to the memo.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: sensitivity analysis. The fleet size is a monotone function of each device parameter; the model's output (number of machines) is the measure of system performance that matters for procurement and scheduling. We examine how each parameter moves the fleet count and the schedule, and rank the research directions by the magnitude of that movement.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Sensitivity of N_eds to each parameter (Airport A, base: 25 EDS, 4230.5 bags): (1) Speed: EDS_RATE 160->185->210 gives N_eds = 29->25->22, a 24% swing across the plausible range; a 10% speed increase (185->203.5) reduces N_eds by 1-2 units. Speed has the largest per-percent effect on fleet count because N_eds is inversely proportional to rate. (2) Reliability: EDS_AVAIL 0.90->0.92->0.95 gives effective rate 144->170.2->185.75 and N_eds = 30->25->23; a 2-point availability gain (0.92->0.94) at rate 185 gives 173.9 eff, N_eds=25 (unchanged at the ceiling), but at the boundary it can save 1 unit; reliability matters most when utilization is near 1.0, which is the design point here, so it is effectively co-equal with speed. (3) Accuracy: RESOLVE 0.985->0.99->0.995 changes alarmed bags from 63.5->42.3->21.2, i.e., the secondary-inspection load (15.9 h->10.6 h->5.3 h at 15 min/bag). Accuracy does not change the EDS fleet count at all; it changes the secondary-staffing requirement. A 0.5-point accuracy gain halves the manual-review load. (4) Cost: EDS_COST does not enter the fleet-count model; it enters the procurement budget and the spare-machine decision. A cost reduction does not change how many machines are needed, only how many can be afforded; it is a budget constraint, not a performance lever, in this model. (5) ETD speed/accuracy: ETA_RATE 40->45->50 gives N_ets at A = 22->20->17; a 10% ETD speed gain saves 1-2 ETDs. ETA_ACC 0.997->0.999 cuts the joint miss rate on the flagged 20% from 1.45e-4 to 8.5e-5, a 41% relative reduction. STEM research priorities, ranked by impact on system performance: (1) Scan-speed improvement (CT reconstruction and detector throughput) - direct, per-percent inverse effect on fleet count; the single highest-leverage investment, because each 10% speed gain retires 1-2 machines per large airport, which scales across 193 airports. (2) Operational reliability (belt, sensor, and software fault reduction) - co-equal with speed at the near-100%-utilization design point; each 2-point availability gain is worth 1-2 machines and removes the single-machine-failure risk that the schedule model shows breaks the hour. (3) Image-resolution / accuracy - largest effect on secondary staffing rather than fleet count; a 0.5-point gain halves manual review, freeing labor that is the binding constraint at 10x cost for ETD. (4) ETD throughput and accuracy - important for the enhanced-screening policy, but the ETD fleet is small, so the absolute fleet-count effect is 1-2 machines per airport. (5) Cost reduction - not a performance lever in this model; it affects the budget envelope and the spare-machine decision, so it is a procurement lever, ranked last for system performance.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo should tell the Director of Homeland Security that the highest-impact STEM investment is scan speed, followed closely by reliability, because both act directly on the machine count that determines the national EDS shortfall. Accuracy is the highest-impact lever on the labor side (secondary and ETD staffing) but not on the machine count. Cost reduction should be funded as a procurement objective, not as a performance objective. The model's limitation here: it treats the parameters as independent, but in practice faster CT scanning may come with a trade-off in resolution (accuracy), and higher availability may require higher maintenance cost; a coupled multi-objective study of the speed-accuracy-reliability-cost surface would refine the ranking. The 2% cancellation and the 92% availability are held at national values; a regional re-estimation would shift the absolute fleet counts but not the sensitivity ordering.
